subtype: Approach: reading the chapter again and again [Action]
passage: In the school library, Karan opened his science chapter and read it once. Then he read it again, slowly, and a third time. He did not underline a single line. He nodded at each page. "I know this," he told himself. "It looks so familiar." He closed the book. Bhavna, a classmate at the next table, asked her own question: "Karan, what are the two kinds of mixtures in chapter four?" He looked at the ceiling and said, "It was on that page with the pictures." Then he opened the book and began the first page again.

qa.q: How many times did Karan read the science chapter?
What was Karan feeling as he closed the book and said "I know this"?
qa.a: He felt sure and confident. The pages looked familiar, so he believed he was ready.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Karan try after Bhavna's question, and why?
qa.a: He could close the book and write down what he remembers from each page. Trying to recall shows what he really knows.

qa.q: How might Bhavna see Karan's answer to her question?
qa.a: Bhavna saw a classmate who could point to the page but not name the answer. She might wonder if he knew the chapter as well as he thought.

grounding: A boy rereads his science chapter three times and feels ready because the words look familiar, though he has only recognised the text and not tried to recall it.

subtype: Approach: reading the chapter again and again [Action]
passage: My brother Santosh had a science test on Tuesday, so on Sunday he sat by the window with the chapter on light. I watched from my bed. He read it from start to end. Then again. Then a third time, lips moving a little. No pencil, no notes, nothing underlined. After the third time he shut the book and said, "Done. I know it all, every page looks familiar." Minakshi Aunty, who was visiting, asked, "Tell me, what is a shadow?" He opened his mouth, then said, "It's in the part with the torch picture." I can't say what he was thinking then, but he didn't open the book again.

qa.q: What might Santosh have felt after the third reading?
qa.a: He seemed confident and relieved, saying every page looked familiar, even though he hadn't tried to recall anything.

qa.q: What else could Santosh try to check whether he really knows it?
qa.a: Close the book and answer questions like Minakshi Aunty's from memory, then check; recognising a page is not the same as recalling it.

qa.q: How might Minakshi Aunty see Santosh's answer about shadows?
qa.a: Minakshi Aunty hears him point to a picture instead of explaining, so she may suspect he recognises the page but can't yet explain it.

grounding: Shows a boy reading his science chapter three times without notes and feeling ready because it looks familiar, though he cannot recall it.

subtype: Approach: reading the chapter again and again [Action]
passage:
Wednesday. Hemant read the science chapter on magnets from the first line to the last. His highlighter lay capped beside him.
Thursday. He read it twice more, once after school and once after dinner. By the third time every diagram looked like an old friend. "I'm ready," he told his friend Santosh on the phone. "I've read it three times."
Friday. The first question asked him to name the two poles and say what happens when like poles meet. Hemant could picture the page, even the red-and-blue drawing in the corner, but the words wouldn't come. He stared at the fan, tapping his pen.

qa.q: What was the science chapter about?
What was Hemant feeling when the words wouldn't come on Friday?
qa.a: He felt stuck and anxious, able to picture the page but not recall the answer, after feeling so ready on Thursday.

qa.q: What would you change first in Hemant's study plan?
qa.a: After one reading, close the book and answer questions like the test's from memory, then check; that shows what he really knows.

qa.q: How might Santosh have heard Hemant's 'I'm ready' on Thursday?
qa.a: Santosh would have heard a confident friend who'd read it three times, with no way of knowing the reading had never been tested.

grounding: Illustrates a boy reading his chapter three times, feeling ready because it looks familiar, and then being unable to recall it in the test.
